passage: After the family rabbit died, Tarun, five, sat quietly beside the empty hutch and stayed close to his father Nilesh all day. That night Nilesh said, "Bunny died. His body stopped working and he won't come back. I'm sad too." Four days later Tarun drew a brown rabbit and asked, "Is he cold?" "No. He doesn't feel anything now." Nine days after that, Tarun asked for his usual bedtime story, then hugged his drawing as he fell asleep.

qa.q: What did Tarun ask on the fourth day?
qa.a: "Is he cold?"

qa.q: What might Tarun be feeling as he sits beside the empty hutch?
qa.a: Sadness and missing his rabbit. Staying close to his father suggests he needs closeness.

qa.q: How did Nilesh help Tarun?
qa.a: He gave short, honest explanations and kept the usual routine, such as the bedtime story.

qa.q: How might Nilesh feel through these days?
qa.a: Sad too, since he said so, and caring enough to answer each question simply.

grounding: Shows a young child showing sorrow after a pet's death through quiet, clinging, a drawing and questions, met with short honest answers and routine.

passage: On moving day the flat was full of boxes and noisy movers. Rehana, five, sat on the bare floor of her room. "Will my window come with us?" she asked her mother Zainab. "Will the tree be at the new house?" Zainab, busy taping a box, stopped and knelt. "The window stays here. I know you'll miss it. The new room has a different window." Rehana said nothing and held her sleeve for the rest of the afternoon.

qa.q: What did Rehana ask about her window?
qa.a: "Will my window come with us?"

qa.q: What might Rehana be feeling about leaving her room?
qa.a: Sadness about leaving, shown by her questions and by holding her mother's sleeve. It may also be mixed with worry about the noise and change.

qa.q: What could help Rehana through the move?
qa.a: Short honest answers and familiar routines, like lunch at the usual time.

qa.q: How might Zainab feel on moving day?
qa.a: Busy and stretched, yet caring, since she stopped taping the box to kneel and answer.

grounding: Shows a young child showing sorrow over a move through questions and clinging, with a parent giving a short honest answer.

passage: Goldie, the fish, was floating when Noor woke up. Jeevan, her father, told her simply: “Goldie died in the night. Her body stopped working. She won't swim again.” Noor was quiet all day, following him from room to room. At dinner she asked, “Will Goldie come back?” “No, sweetheart. But we can remember her.” That night, they buried Goldie in the balcony pot, and Noor drew a gold fish on a card. Jeevan kept bedtime the same: bath, story, song.

qa.q: Where did they bury Goldie?
qa.a: In the balcony pot.

qa.q: What was Noor feeling as she followed her father from room to room?
qa.a: She was sad and a bit unsettled after losing Goldie, and wanted to stay close to him.

qa.q: Why did Jeevan keep bedtime the same?
qa.a: A familiar routine helps a grieving child feel safe, alongside short, honest answers.

qa.q: How might Jeevan feel answering Noor's question about Goldie?
qa.a: He likely feels tender and sad for her, but chooses to be honest and gentle.

grounding: A preschooler is quiet and clingy after her fish dies, and her father gives short honest answers and keeps the routine.

passage:
“Dadu, when are we going home?”
“This is our home now, Pema. In the city.”
“I mean real home. With the hills.”
Jagdish put down his newspaper. Pema had been quiet since the move, clinging to his kurta.
“You miss the hills.”
“And my friend. And our dog.”
“I miss them too. We live here now. But we can call your friend on Sunday.”
Pema leaned on him. “Can we have a dog here?”
“Let's think about it. Now, it's time for your bath, same as always.”

qa.q: When did Dadu say they could call Pema's friend?
qa.a: On Sunday.

qa.q: What was Pema feeling as she clung to Dadu's kurta?
qa.a: She was sad and homesick for the hills, her friend and their dog.

qa.q: How did Jagdish support Pema without a long talk?
qa.a: He named her feeling, gave a short honest answer, offered a Sunday call and kept her routine with bath time.

qa.q: How might Jagdish feel when Pema says she misses the hills?
qa.a: He likely feels sad too, since he admits he misses them, but stays steady for her.

grounding: A preschooler shows sorrow after moving house, and her grandfather gives short honest explanations and keeps routine.

passage:
Note by Chaitanya, nursery teacher.
Suraj's dog died on the weekend. This week he has been quiet and clingy, staying close to me at play. Today he drew a brown dog with wings and asked, “Does it hurt to die?” I said, “No. When a body stops working, it doesn't feel pain anymore.” He nodded and coloured the wings. I kept his day the same as usual: circle, snack, sandpit. I've told his parents about the drawing and the question so they can talk at home.

qa.q: What did Suraj draw on the dog?
qa.a: Wings.

qa.q: What was Suraj feeling as he stayed close at play?
qa.a: He was sad and a little lost after his dog died, and staying close felt safer.

qa.q: Why was Chaitanya's short answer helpful?
qa.a: A short, honest answer met Suraj's real question without overwhelming him, and the usual routine kept him steady.

qa.q: How might Suraj's parents feel reading the note?
qa.a: They'd likely feel grateful to know about his question and drawing, so they can support him at home.

grounding: The teacher's note shows a preschooler's sorrow in drawing and questions after his dog died, met with short honest answers and routine.

passage:
Since Moti died, Jasleen had stopped running to the gate when the milk van came. She held the end of Mummy's dupatta wherever Mummy went, even to the cowshed. At night she drew a brown dog with a very big tail.

"Will Moti come back after the harvest?"

Mummy knelt. "No, beta. Moti's body stopped working, and he can't come back. We can miss him together."

Next morning Mummy still sent her to feed the hens, as always. Imran from the flour mill next door waved. Jasleen waved back, just a little.

qa.q: What did Jasleen draw at night?
qa.a: A brown dog with a very big tail.

qa.q: What does Jasleen holding the end of Mummy's dupatta suggest she was feeling?
qa.a: She was most likely sad and a bit insecure after losing Moti, wanting to stay close to Mummy. Her question about the harvest shows she may also be confused about where Moti went.

qa.q: Why did Mummy's short, honest answer help more than a long talk?
qa.a: It gave Jasleen a clear truth she could hold on to, and keeping her usual job of feeding the hens gave her day something steady.

qa.q: How might Imran see Jasleen's small wave?
qa.a: Imran may notice she is quieter than before, but a small wave back is a sign she is slowly returning to her usual self.

grounding: It shows a young child's quiet, clingy sorrow after a pet dies, eased by a short honest explanation and a familiar routine.
